World.title: How this Sydney private school asked students to help solve the consent crisis
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWEducation How this Sydney private school asked students to help solve the consent crisis Emily Kowal August 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One glance up from her desk reminds principal Julie McGonigle of the utter destruction caused by unchecked gendered stereotypes and violence. On her wall hangs a circle of eucalyptus leaves painted blue, an artwork created on the day sports coach Lilie James was murdered by a colleague and former boyfriend inside the toilets of St Andrew’s Cathedral School in 2023. A twin work in pink hangs in James’ childhood bedroom. It symbolises the circle of support that comes after tragedy. Principal Julie McGonigle with year 12 students Ruby Buckman and Lachlan Sparshott, who sit on a student-led panel to help shape St Andrew’s Cathedral School’s approach to respectful relationships education. KATE GERAGHTY It’s a stark reminder that violence against women starts small: tracking location on Snapchat. A sexist joke on Instagram. They may seem like low-level infractions, but this school has seen first-hand where they can lead. It is a crisis echoing across the city. Following a series of sexual assaults by students in Sydney schools, including Scots College, educators and parents are rethinking their approach to respectful relationships, while advocates have called for greater control over social media algorithms.



In the aftermath of the tragedy, McGonigle commissioned a review of international best practice on respectful relationships education and prevention of gender-based violence. The research stressed that schools must design their responses with students. Students must feel safe to have open conversations about difficult topics such as coercive control, pornography and relationships. “Their lived experience now makes them part of the solution because they have seen first-hand the pure devastation that is caused,” McGonigle said. “This idea of compassionate accountability is about holding people to account, but still maintaining openness.” Julie McGonigle, St Andrew’s Cathedral School principal She formed a panel of experts including student representatives who meet quarterly to discuss coercive control, relationships, pornography and harmful online content. Year 12 students Ruby Buckman and Lachlan Sparshott both sit on that panel as representatives of the student body, helping to shape what respectful relationships education looks like in classrooms.



Ruby said the school’s inclusive approach meant education should be created “with young people, not just for them”, so students feel ownership and are more likely to engage. Lachlan said the school has become more open. “It opened up a conversation where people feel very comfortable amidst friends, teachers and parents to talk about these topics.” St Andrew’s students are explicitly taught to recognise patterns of coercive control and abuse. Principal Julie McGonigle (centre) with school captains Ruby Buckman and Lachlan Sparshott. KATE GERAGHTY At St Andrew’s, students are explicitly taught to recognise patterns of coercive control and technology-facilitated abuse, such as tracking one another on Snapchat. Students are pushed to think critically about online content. In a letter to students sent after the conclusion of the coronial inquest into James’ death, McGonigle issued explicit advice.



“Small things matter – sexist jokes and unwanted comments are not harmless ‘banter’. Call it out, interrupt it, seek support so that a harmful culture doesn’t develop,” McGonigle wrote in a letter to students. “There isn’t one ideal way to be a man or a woman – there are as many ways as there are personalities.” Editor's pick Consent crisis ‘Blatant misogyny’: Ex-Scots student despairs of school culture The urgency of this work is backed by a University of Melbourne study, released last week, which found young Australians hold more violent and hostile attitudes towards women than any other generation, and that these views are metastasising in classrooms across the country. Almost one in three boys aged between 13 and 17 believe attempts to give women equal opportunities have gone too far, the study found, while one in four believe feminism is damaging to society and should be resisted with violence if necessary. The study found these attitudes were associated with the online content young people were consuming. “Engagement with ‘manosphere’ content, pornography and online dating showed the strongest links to misogynistic views,” lead author Dr Sara Meger said.



Youth educator Daniel Principe travels to schools to deliver workshops on healthy masculinity and consent. The other day a young boy asked him an earnest question: “How do you control a wife?” Principe did not shame the boy. Instead, he used it as an opening to unpack where the student had learnt the premise. Principe encourages such questions. “We know that young people have already been exposed to pretty horrific ideas. We owe it to them to actually give them an opportunity to think through these things.” At St Andrews, the school champions “compassionate accountability”. “If boys feel like they’re the enemy – they’re the problem in society, all of them are violent offenders – you end up hardening a whole generation’s attitudes. The shutters come down, and you’re not getting anywhere. So this idea of compassionate accountability is about holding people to account, but still maintaining openness,” McGonigle said. Principe warned this problem was not isolated to private schools, nor did he want schools to carry the weight of this scourge.



“These are cultural challenges. They are happening in all schools in all postcodes. I haven’t been to a school that hasn’t been impacted by these horrific attitudes,” Principe said. Another perspective Opinion

Crime This moment crystallises a very uncomfortable truth about sexual violence Natassia Chrysanthos Federal political correspondent “We’re actually doing more than we ever have. The difference is, we’re fighting against horrific industries who have made this challenge harder than ever before. We’re dealing with the fact that young people have been exposed to horrific content, influences, pornography online, well before quite often an adult at home or at school has had a healthy, constructive conversation with them.” St Andrews does not have all the solutions. “There’s no silver bullets, and it’s not a quick fix,” McGonigle said. “You can’t just say ‘I’ve got three consent lectures, and I’ve nailed it’.” Instead, she argues, it takes a connected and secure community, a culture that encourages students to stand up and intervene when they see low-level controlling behaviours.



Those who lived through 2023 were permanently changed, nor has the grief from the loss of Lilie diminished with time. “She was greatly loved and brought life, colour and vitality to our school,” McGonigle said. World.title: An AI track almost topped the ARIA charts. Now only AI ‘assisted’ songs will be allowed
World.content:
CultureMusicAI An AI track almost topped the ARIA charts. Now only AI ‘assisted’ songs will be allowed Kayla Olaya August 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The organisation in charge of Australia’s pop music charts has announced a ban on tunes made wholly by AI, but some say it does not go far enough to protect local music. The Australian Recording Industry Association will allow AI-assisted songs that have lead vocals, lyrics and primary instruments created and performed by humans to continue to top charts. Meanwhile, tunes “substantially” made using AI will not be allowed. ARIA has issued new rules on AI songs. Aresna Villanueva ARIA attracted criticism after an AI cover of Madonna’s hit 1989 song Like a Prayer by Josh Fawaz began topping its chart in May. The song’s credits on Spotify state that it uses generative AI for vocals and drums. It peaked at No.2 at the time of release and has spent 16 weeks in the top 10. As of August 24, the song sits at No.4 on the chart. The track also appears on commercial radio as an Australian song, which helps stations fulfil obligations to promote 25 per cent Australian music – without paying the royalties.



ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said while her association “can’t control what people listen to”, the new policy was made to ensure that the tunes that appear on the charts are “substantially human-made”. “We also don’t want to be celebrating or encouraging tracks that are recorded using AI tools that have stolen music to train their AI systems,” Herd said. ARIA’s three new categories AI-generated: Not eligible Generative AI produced the recording, or the primary part of its creative elements. A lead vocal or a key instrumental performance generated by AI puts a recording here.

AI-assisted: Eligible Humans wrote the song and performed the lead vocal and the primary instruments. Generative AI did something minor on top of that.

AI in production: Eligible AI mastering, AI drum machines, stem separation, reverb or instrument patches that a person then plays are considered OK.

“It’s fine to use AI in your music creation … We’re not saying that that is going to be banned from the chart but we’re saying that tracks that are not substantially human [will be banned].” The singer-songwriter Jack River, whose real name is Holly Rankin, said the changes were an important step for Australia’s music industry and had opened up a conversation about how “human” music can be in an era of AI.



Related Article Live music It took James years to master a single note. Now he’s being replaced by technology “I really back it because it means that we’re putting human artistry and human creativity first,” Rankin said. “I don’t think anybody wants to go and see an AI agent performing at Groovin’ the Moo. “We do need to have a conversation about what constitutes music, human-created music, and it’s a very strange reality we’re living in … I think we have that responsibility as artists to tell audiences what’s in our [music]. And our peak body needs to protect the real, human music economy behind this.” Violinist James Steendam, the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA) union’s federal president of musicians, said that while ARIA’s announcement was a step in the right direction for artists, theft of their work and creative output by AI companies continued “unabated, and this voluntary code of practice will not stop that”. “The ARIA Charts Code of Practice is voluntary, so can only go so far … MEAA is calling on the federal government to step in and mandate labelling of AI-generated content across music and the creative sector,” said Steendam, who believes he was replaced by a synthesising technology in musical theatre production The Lion King.



When filling out the survey to submit a song to ARIA, artists will now have to tick a box stating whether they’ve used AI in the track, and whether it was AI-generated or AI-assisted. “The range of AI-assisted actions permitted is too broad and includes synthesising backing vocals, strings, brass and other instruments. This undercuts session musicians or non-featured artists.” Olivia Dean performs at the ARIA Awards in 2025. Getty Images In March, a North Carolina man pleaded guilty to defrauding music streaming platforms and musicians out of millions in royalties by flooding them with thousands of AI-generated songs and later using “bots” to boost licensing numbers. In July, Spotify announced it was being inundated with AI-generated songs, and that it had removed more than 75 million spam tracks.





Walsh says the licensing component was important to embed in ARIA’s code as it puts pressure on AI companies developing tools to license content. “It will make content that’s not generated without that licensing less valuable because it won’t be going up the charts, the ARIA charts, and therefore won’t be getting the same attention as content that is generated with that,” he said. “Even if it’s only psychological, even if it’s only a case of showing where their support is, even if it had no material impact upon the AI companies, I would still support the idea that they should be backing artists … [ARIA] had an opportunity to make a statement,” Walsh said. Asked if ARIA would adopt the IFPI’s guidelines on AI tools and licensed content, Herd said: “We definitely support that in principle, and we have provisions in our code that include unlawful activity, unlawful tracks, unlawful tools. If we become aware of something like that then we can act on that as well”. Steendam said artists and musicians currently have no share in the licensing arrangements between record labels and AI companies, “nor any right to refuse for their work to be used in this way”.



The changes take effect in the ARIA charts from Monday, August 31. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: NRL’s latest rule-change adds a new element of strategy. Here’s how it will work
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL’s latest rule-change adds a new element of strategy. Here’s how it will work Adrian Proszenko August 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Players rather than coaches will dictate how the NRL’s experiment with a change to the kick-off rule is conducted when Brisbane and Melbourne road-test it for the first time on Thursday night. Rugby league could be getting a glimpse into its future when the match between last year’s grand finalists is played under a new rule giving the team that concedes points the option to either kick off or receive the football from the resumption. Loading The rule tweak will be trialled in matches with no bearing on the finals over the remainder of the season, beginning with Thursday night’s Storm-Broncos clash at Suncorp Stadium. The change could result in fewer blowouts, given the scoring team won’t necessarily retain possession after the re-start. Much will come down to the tactics employed, although it’s expected the decisions will be made on the field rather than in the coach’s box.



“We will very much leave it to [captain] Harry [Grant] to make the call,” said Melbourne’s director of football, Frank Ponissi. “The proposed way it’s going to be handled by the NRL – and we agree with this – the referee will immediately ask the captain what he would like to do. He won’t have any time to get any decision from the coaches via the trainer or any other way, it will be very similar to the captain’s challenge. A proposed change to the kick-off rule will be trialled on Thursday night. Getty Images “We will trust our captain, our players and leaders on the field to come up with the right decision at the time … “[Not having coaching input] is a good thing, and we support that. It gets rid of delays in the game, otherwise you’re waiting for the trainer to run on and get a message. The last thing we want as a game is stoppages like that … Ultimately, it’s fantastic we’re letting the players decide what they are doing.”



Troy Thomson, Brisbane’s manager of football operations, said the rule tweak would provide a lever that could allow momentum to be shifted. “We’ll brief the players and the captain in particular, working through different scenarios,” Thompson said. “If you get scored on, you probably want to get the footy back, particularly if you are chasing points as well. It will depend on the circumstances. If it’s the back end of the game, your tactics and strategy will be very different at the start of the game. It will be quite situational. Dragons captain Damien Cook will play under the new rule in the final-round clash against Parramatta. NRL Photos “It adds another level of strategy for the players.” A point of interest will be whether a team chasing points opts to receive the ball or instead attempts to regather it from a short kick-off. It could also pose a dilemma for teams in front as the clock winds down.



“If you’re protecting a lead with not long to go, sometimes territory is better than possession,” Ponissi explained. “You may as well kick it down [the field], especially with how teams are doing short kick-offs so well. You’d run the threat of losing the ball and giving very good attacking position to the opposition.” The NRL will have a relatively small sample size before deciding to implement the change permanently from next season. The only other confirmed trial in a “dead rubber” is the final-round clash between the Eels and Dragons. “I’m going to want the ball back in my hands if we’ve been scored against to stop the momentum,” said Dragons captain Damien Cook. “A team like Penrith that are very good at their yardage D [defence], they might see a chance to kick off again, lock them back in there and get good field position straight away … “If you’re a team in front and dominating the game, you may want to kick off again. If you’ve got the momentum against you, you probably want the ball back in your hands.”



Related Article NRL 2026 NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night The merits of the change have divided the game. While seven-time premiership-winning coach Wayne Bennett has been a vocal proponent, others believe it is unnecessarily tampering with the fabric of the game. Speaking on Nine’s 100% Footy, Phil Gould and Paul Gallen said they wanted the status quo to remain. “Honestly, this is ridiculous,” Gallen said. “We don’t need all these rule changes. The game’s been so good for such a long time, I don’t get this one.” Gould said that when made in the Super League, the change had only made blowouts worse.



“If you win the toss in a big game, what’s the first thing you say? We’ll kick off. Why? Because it’s easier to get down the other end,” Gould said. “Now you’re going to make it harder for the other team to get down the end.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Police cleared of manslaughter over man’s traffic arrest death
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Police cleared of manslaughter over man’s traffic arrest death Tara Cosoleto August 25, 2026 — 7:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Manslaughter charges against two police officers have been thrown out by a magistrate who said the case bore no comparison to the death in the United States of George Floyd. Builder Luke Briggs, 35, died eight days after he was arrested in a convenience store car park at Hoppers Crossing, in Melbourne’s west, in July 2024. Sergeant James Fitzgerald (centre) and Constable Alexander Papanastassis pictured last September. Simon Schluter Constable Alexander Papanastassis, 30, and Sergeant James Fitzgerald, 46, were each charged with negligent manslaughter over the death but fought the charges at a preliminary hearing. Magistrate Patrick Southey determined on Tuesday that there was insufficient evidence for the case to go to trial and dismissed the charges.



“The evidence is so weak that the prospect of a conviction is minimal,” Southey said. “It may be the manner in which Mr Briggs was restrained was the substantial and operative cause of death, but we’ll never know.” Luke Briggs, pictured with sister Catherine, died in July 2024. Briggs became unresponsive during the arrest and the officers performed CPR while waiting for paramedics. The 35-year-old died in hospital on July 23, eight days after his arrest, surrounded by family. Photos at the time showed bruising on his arms as he lay in a hospital bed. In delivering his ruling, Southey referred to the high-profile case of African-American man George Floyd in the US. Floyd was murdered by a white police officer who was arresting him in May 2020.



His dying words of “I can’t breathe” were also said by Briggs, the magistrate noted. “It seems to me the parallels end there,” Southey said. Related Article Victoria Police conduct Family sues police over death of 35-year-old builder in custody “There is no comparison to this case where ... the police were doing the best they could. It was not a perfect job but the best they could do in all the circumstances.” The magistrate noted Briggs was a large, powerful man whose behaviour had been irrational due to methamphetamine use.



“It was an unfortunate, tragic chain of events, but in my view, it does not amount to criminal negligence,” Southey said in the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court. He awarded costs to Papanastassis and Fitzgerald, who have both been suspended from duties since the incident. Members of Briggs’s family were visibly upset as the decision was handed down. Family and friends of Luke Briggs gather to mark the first anniversary of his death. Eddie Jim The family is separately suing the state, accusing the officers of breaching their duty of care and Victoria Police of failing to “properly supervise, control or train their employees, officers and/or agents”.



Police Association secretary Wayne Gatt said the union had stood by the members who had now been rightfully cleared.



“Our members did their job. A difficult job, a challenging job, a dynamic job, and one that places them squarely between criminal behaviour and community safety,” he said.



“That night, they did what any of their colleagues would have done. They pulled over a suspicious vehicle and attempted to speak to the driver. When the situation escalated into a physical confrontation, they tried to manage it peacefully, but they were not afforded that opportunity.” AAP

World.title: Rabbitoh closes in on three-year deal; concussed Radley set to miss rest of regular season
World.content:
Tallis Duncan says he is ready to shift back to his preferred back-row position to accommodate Latrell Mitchell as he prepares to sign off on a contract extension that is set to keep him at the club until the end 2030. Duncan has been impressive in the centres in the three months Mitchell has been sidelined with injury. Tallis Duncan is a star on the rise at Souths. Getty Images Mitchell, who has had nerve issues in his lower back and related problems in his leg and calf, was named in the No.19 jersey for Saturday’s clash against the Gold Coast. Duncan, 24, has been one of the Bunnies’ best this season, and his form is expected to be rewarded with a new three-year deal.



The 24-year-old was ready to attract plenty of interest had he remained a free agent until November 1, but made it clear he was only interested in remaining in the red and green – and there was one rival club he would never entertain. “I want to be here, this is where I want to be – I see myself as a South Sydney player for a long time,” Duncan said. Loading “I was a Roosters junior, but [a return to the Roosters] won’t be happening. There’s some history there. I won’t say too much about it, but that won’t happen.” Duncan said Mitchell’s impending return to the line-up would give the Bunnies a timely boost leading into a likely finals campaign. “It’s massive for us as a club,” Duncan said. “You know what he brings: his presence, he brings confidence [to the rest of us]. He’s the ace up our sleeve.”



Meanwhile, Roosters skipper James Tedesco (ankle) has been named to return from an ankle injury for Saturday’s match of the round against the Dolphins, with Nat Butcher to start at lock for Victor Radley. Radley suffered his eighth concussion in five years during the shock loss to the Wests Tigers and will miss the Dolphins blockbuster due to the NRL’s mandatory 11-day stand-down, but was in good spirits at training on Tuesday. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 ‘I’ll cry my eyes out’: Jai Arrow will take the field for South Sydney again. Expect tears Daly Cherry-Evans said Radley’s latest head knock may even prove a blessing for the no-nonsense forward. “He was fine today, which is a really good sign,” Cherry-Evans said. “I know he’s in very good hands at this club. The Roosters take a lot of pride in how they handle serious situations like head injuries. There are no short-cuts or sweeping anything under the carpet – it’s always about the best interests of the player.



“It’s a case-by-case scenario, but I’ve heard ‘Robbo’ [coach Trent Robinson] talk about it publicly before, and he’s really clear on how it should be handled. “Rads is a leader of our side, he’s one of the elite locks in the game. We know how classy his ball playing is, but his defence this year has been great for us. If it’s not as bad as like he was telling me this morning, that’s a great freshen-up for Rads going into the finals.” Radley sidelined with concussion Christian Nicolussi Victor Radley looks set to be sidelined until the finals after suffering a concussion during the Roosters’ stunning 25-24 loss to Wests Tigers on Sunday.



The Roosters confirmed on Monday Radley had displayed category one symptoms after a heavy collision, which means he will need to stand down for the next 11 days. Loading Radley went low on Tigers forward Alex Seyfarth and wobbled back into the defensive line before referee Ashley Klein realised the seriousness of the situation and sent him for a head injury assessment. The tackle happened in the 79th minute, just before Jock Madden kicked the match-winning field goal, meaning Radley’s condition was missed by many observers at full-time. Fans initially feared Radley would miss Saturday’s clash with the Dolphins due to a high tackle on Patrick Herbert. He was charged by the match review committee on Monday but only fined $3000.



But the concussion will mean he misses the Dolphins clash and most likely the round-27 showdown with South Sydney on Friday week. Victor Radley comes from the field after being concussed against the Broncos in 2025. Getty Images Given his long history of head knocks – Sunday was his eighth concussion or failed HIA in five years – Radley will now be required to gain a clearance from an independent doctor to play again. The Roosters have adopted an ultra-conservative approach with players returning from concussions, including Lindsay Collins, who was given six weeks to recover earlier this season – a break which also cost him a chance to play for Queensland in the Origin decider. Related Article NRL 2026 NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night



Skipper and fullback James Tedesco is hoping to return from an ankle injury for the Allianz Stadium hit-out, which the Dolphins need to win to remain in the top four. Radley last year said he had no plans to retire early, revealing he met with several specialists and even started playing memory games twice a day to “work” his brain. “I’ve got no worries whatsoever with my head,” Radley said at the time. The 28-year-old Bronte local is eager to help the Roosters win the premiership, then turn his attention to helping England win the World Cup. Siua Wong was also charged with a careless high tackle on Jock Madden, but can also escape with a fine, while Reece Robson and Daly Cherry-Evans were not cited by the match review committee, despite being placed on report for a high tackle and trip.



Ten Dogs struck down by COVID Dan Walsh Ten Bulldogs NRL squad members – headlined by star back-rower Jacob Preston – were kept away from the club training on Monday as a COVID-19 outbreak threatens to derail the biggest week of Canterbury’s season. Just five days out from Friday’s must-win clash against powerhouse Penrith, the Bulldogs trained without more than a quarter of their NRL squad (which includes top 30 and development players) after a spate of positive COVID-19 tests among their players. Preston was the most notable absentee, while fellow forwards Josh Curran and Kurt Mann were also missing – though Mann was carrying a groin injury that was expected to rule him out of selection against the Panthers. Not all the players taken ill are first-graders.



Assistant coach Adam O’Brien was also told to stay at home after flu ripped through the club for a second straight week. Jacob Preston in action against the Dragons on Saturday night. NRL Photos Preston’s positive COVID-19 test came after the barnstorming second-rower spent time in hospital on a drip last week due to an elbow infection, in the days leading into the 44-14 win over St George Illawarra that kept Canterbury’s season alive. Coach Cameron Ciraldo revealed after downing the Dragons match that five players had missed training throughout the week due to COVID-19 as well. It is unclear at this stage how the outbreak will impact Ciraldo’s team list announcement for the Panthers clash, which must be announced at 4pm on Tuesday, but the club is taking no chances and keeping any player showing symptoms away from their Belmore base.



The ninth-placed Bulldogs will have their main field session on Wednesday. Winger Enari Tuala, who was a late scratching last week with a knee injury, is expected to return against the Panthers, while Jacob Kiraz continues to push through a calf injury. Loading With two rounds left in the regular season, a loss to Penrith would almost certainly end Canterbury’s hopes of sneaking into the top eight given the Cowboys (eighth) and South Sydney (seventh) already sit two points ahead of them on the ladder. Last year’s corresponding clash between the sides saw Panthers coach Ivan Cleary rest his entire first choice teams. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 People feared the Chiefs would be a joke. The NRL might have created a monster instead Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist



But with Penrith still fighting to secure a home final, Cleary will name his best line-up on Friday night before weighing up whether to do the same a week later against the Tigers in the last game of the regular season. Jack Cole is expected to replace suspended five-eighth Jack Cogger against the Bulldogs given Blaize Talagi’s defensive frailties were exposed by Canterbury’s right edge earlier this year.

World.title: How this Sydney private school asked students to help solve the consent crisis
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWEducation How this Sydney private school asked students to help solve the consent crisis Emily Kowal August 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One glance up from her desk reminds principal Julie McGonigle of the utter destruction caused by unchecked gendered stereotypes and violence. On her wall hangs a circle of eucalyptus leaves painted blue, an artwork created on the day sports coach Lilie James was murdered by a colleague and former boyfriend inside the toilets of St Andrew’s Cathedral School in 2023. A twin work in pink hangs in James’ childhood bedroom. It symbolises the circle of support that comes after tragedy. Principal Julie McGonigle with year 12 students Ruby Buckman and Lachlan Sparshott, who sit on a student-led panel to help shape St Andrew’s Cathedral School’s approach to respectful relationships education. KATE GERAGHTY It’s a stark reminder that violence against women starts small: tracking location on Snapchat. A sexist joke on Instagram. They may seem like low-level infractions, but this school has seen first-hand where they can lead. It is a crisis echoing across the city. Following a series of sexual assaults by students in Sydney schools, including Scots College, educators and parents are rethinking their approach to respectful relationships, while advocates have called for greater control over social media algorithms.



In the aftermath of the tragedy, McGonigle commissioned a review of international best practice on respectful relationships education and prevention of gender-based violence. The research stressed that schools must design their responses with students. Students must feel safe to have open conversations about difficult topics such as coercive control, pornography and relationships. “Their lived experience now makes them part of the solution because they have seen first-hand the pure devastation that is caused,” McGonigle said. “This idea of compassionate accountability is about holding people to account, but still maintaining openness.” Julie McGonigle, St Andrew’s Cathedral School principal She formed a panel of experts including student representatives who meet quarterly to discuss coercive control, relationships, pornography and harmful online content. Year 12 students Ruby Buckman and Lachlan Sparshott both sit on that panel as representatives of the student body, helping to shape what respectful relationships education looks like in classrooms.



Ruby said the school’s inclusive approach meant education should be created “with young people, not just for them”, so students feel ownership and are more likely to engage. Lachlan said the school has become more open. “It opened up a conversation where people feel very comfortable amidst friends, teachers and parents to talk about these topics.” St Andrew’s students are explicitly taught to recognise patterns of coercive control and abuse. Principal Julie McGonigle (centre) with school captains Ruby Buckman and Lachlan Sparshott. KATE GERAGHTY At St Andrew’s, students are explicitly taught to recognise patterns of coercive control and technology-facilitated abuse, such as tracking one another on Snapchat. Students are pushed to think critically about online content. In a letter to students sent after the conclusion of the coronial inquest into James’ death, McGonigle issued explicit advice.



“Small things matter – sexist jokes and unwanted comments are not harmless ‘banter’. Call it out, interrupt it, seek support so that a harmful culture doesn’t develop,” McGonigle wrote in a letter to students. “There isn’t one ideal way to be a man or a woman – there are as many ways as there are personalities.” Editor's pick Consent crisis ‘Blatant misogyny’: Ex-Scots student despairs of school culture The urgency of this work is backed by a University of Melbourne study, released last week, which found young Australians hold more violent and hostile attitudes towards women than any other generation, and that these views are metastasising in classrooms across the country. Almost one in three boys aged between 13 and 17 believe attempts to give women equal opportunities have gone too far, the study found, while one in four believe feminism is damaging to society and should be resisted with violence if necessary. The study found these attitudes were associated with the online content young people were consuming. “Engagement with ‘manosphere’ content, pornography and online dating showed the strongest links to misogynistic views,” lead author Dr Sara Meger said.



Youth educator Daniel Principe travels to schools to deliver workshops on healthy masculinity and consent. The other day a young boy asked him an earnest question: “How do you control a wife?” Principe did not shame the boy. Instead, he used it as an opening to unpack where the student had learnt the premise. Principe encourages such questions. “We know that young people have already been exposed to pretty horrific ideas. We owe it to them to actually give them an opportunity to think through these things.” At St Andrews, the school champions “compassionate accountability”. “If boys feel like they’re the enemy – they’re the problem in society, all of them are violent offenders – you end up hardening a whole generation’s attitudes. The shutters come down, and you’re not getting anywhere. So this idea of compassionate accountability is about holding people to account, but still maintaining openness,” McGonigle said. Principe warned this problem was not isolated to private schools, nor did he want schools to carry the weight of this scourge.



“These are cultural challenges. They are happening in all schools in all postcodes. I haven’t been to a school that hasn’t been impacted by these horrific attitudes,” Principe said. Another perspective Opinion

Crime This moment crystallises a very uncomfortable truth about sexual violence Natassia Chrysanthos Federal political correspondent “We’re actually doing more than we ever have. The difference is, we’re fighting against horrific industries who have made this challenge harder than ever before. We’re dealing with the fact that young people have been exposed to horrific content, influences, pornography online, well before quite often an adult at home or at school has had a healthy, constructive conversation with them.” St Andrews does not have all the solutions. “There’s no silver bullets, and it’s not a quick fix,” McGonigle said. “You can’t just say ‘I’ve got three consent lectures, and I’ve nailed it’.” Instead, she argues, it takes a connected and secure community, a culture that encourages students to stand up and intervene when they see low-level controlling behaviours.



Those who lived through 2023 were permanently changed, nor has the grief from the loss of Lilie diminished with time. “She was greatly loved and brought life, colour and vitality to our school,” McGonigle said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: An AI track almost topped the ARIA charts. Now only AI ‘assisted’ songs will be allowed
World.content:
CultureMusicAI An AI track almost topped the ARIA charts. Now only AI ‘assisted’ songs will be allowed Kayla Olaya August 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The organisation in charge of Australia’s pop music charts has announced a ban on tunes made wholly by AI, but some say it does not go far enough to protect local music. The Australian Recording Industry Association will allow AI-assisted songs that have lead vocals, lyrics and primary instruments created and performed by humans to continue to top charts. Meanwhile, tunes “substantially” made using AI will not be allowed. ARIA has issued new rules on AI songs. Aresna Villanueva ARIA attracted criticism after an AI cover of Madonna’s hit 1989 song Like a Prayer by Josh Fawaz began topping its chart in May. The song’s credits on Spotify state that it uses generative AI for vocals and drums. It peaked at No.2 at the time of release and has spent 16 weeks in the top 10. As of August 24, the song sits at No.4 on the chart. The track also appears on commercial radio as an Australian song, which helps stations fulfil obligations to promote 25 per cent Australian music – without paying the royalties.



ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said while her association “can’t control what people listen to”, the new policy was made to ensure that the tunes that appear on the charts are “substantially human-made”. “We also don’t want to be celebrating or encouraging tracks that are recorded using AI tools that have stolen music to train their AI systems,” Herd said. ARIA’s three new categories AI-generated: Not eligible Generative AI produced the recording, or the primary part of its creative elements. A lead vocal or a key instrumental performance generated by AI puts a recording here.

AI-assisted: Eligible Humans wrote the song and performed the lead vocal and the primary instruments. Generative AI did something minor on top of that.

AI in production: Eligible AI mastering, AI drum machines, stem separation, reverb or instrument patches that a person then plays are considered OK.

“It’s fine to use AI in your music creation … We’re not saying that that is going to be banned from the chart but we’re saying that tracks that are not substantially human [will be banned].” The singer-songwriter Jack River, whose real name is Holly Rankin, said the changes were an important step for Australia’s music industry and had opened up a conversation about how “human” music can be in an era of AI.



Related Article Live music It took James years to master a single note. Now he’s being replaced by technology “I really back it because it means that we’re putting human artistry and human creativity first,” Rankin said. “I don’t think anybody wants to go and see an AI agent performing at Groovin’ the Moo. “We do need to have a conversation about what constitutes music, human-created music, and it’s a very strange reality we’re living in … I think we have that responsibility as artists to tell audiences what’s in our [music]. And our peak body needs to protect the real, human music economy behind this.” Violinist James Steendam, the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA) union’s federal president of musicians, said that while ARIA’s announcement was a step in the right direction for artists, theft of their work and creative output by AI companies continued “unabated, and this voluntary code of practice will not stop that”. “The ARIA Charts Code of Practice is voluntary, so can only go so far … MEAA is calling on the federal government to step in and mandate labelling of AI-generated content across music and the creative sector,” said Steendam, who believes he was replaced by a synthesising technology in musical theatre production The Lion King.



When filling out the survey to submit a song to ARIA, artists will now have to tick a box stating whether they’ve used AI in the track, and whether it was AI-generated or AI-assisted. “The range of AI-assisted actions permitted is too broad and includes synthesising backing vocals, strings, brass and other instruments. This undercuts session musicians or non-featured artists.” Olivia Dean performs at the ARIA Awards in 2025. Getty Images In March, a North Carolina man pleaded guilty to defrauding music streaming platforms and musicians out of millions in royalties by flooding them with thousands of AI-generated songs and later using “bots” to boost licensing numbers. In July, Spotify announced it was being inundated with AI-generated songs, and that it had removed more than 75 million spam tracks.





Walsh says the licensing component was important to embed in ARIA’s code as it puts pressure on AI companies developing tools to license content. “It will make content that’s not generated without that licensing less valuable because it won’t be going up the charts, the ARIA charts, and therefore won’t be getting the same attention as content that is generated with that,” he said. “Even if it’s only psychological, even if it’s only a case of showing where their support is, even if it had no material impact upon the AI companies, I would still support the idea that they should be backing artists … [ARIA] had an opportunity to make a statement,” Walsh said. Asked if ARIA would adopt the IFPI’s guidelines on AI tools and licensed content, Herd said: “We definitely support that in principle, and we have provisions in our code that include unlawful activity, unlawful tracks, unlawful tools. If we become aware of something like that then we can act on that as well”. Steendam said artists and musicians currently have no share in the licensing arrangements between record labels and AI companies, “nor any right to refuse for their work to be used in this way”.



The changes take effect in the ARIA charts from Monday, August 31. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: NRL’s latest rule-change adds a new element of strategy. Here’s how it will work
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL’s latest rule-change adds a new element of strategy. Here’s how it will work Adrian Proszenko August 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Players rather than coaches will dictate how the NRL’s experiment with a change to the kick-off rule is conducted when Brisbane and Melbourne road-test it for the first time on Thursday night. Rugby league could be getting a glimpse into its future when the match between last year’s grand finalists is played under a new rule giving the team that concedes points the option to either kick off or receive the football from the resumption. Loading The rule tweak will be trialled in matches with no bearing on the finals over the remainder of the season, beginning with Thursday night’s Storm-Broncos clash at Suncorp Stadium. The change could result in fewer blowouts, given the scoring team won’t necessarily retain possession after the re-start. Much will come down to the tactics employed, although it’s expected the decisions will be made on the field rather than in the coach’s box.



“We will very much leave it to [captain] Harry [Grant] to make the call,” said Melbourne’s director of football, Frank Ponissi. “The proposed way it’s going to be handled by the NRL – and we agree with this – the referee will immediately ask the captain what he would like to do. He won’t have any time to get any decision from the coaches via the trainer or any other way, it will be very similar to the captain’s challenge. A proposed change to the kick-off rule will be trialled on Thursday night. Getty Images “We will trust our captain, our players and leaders on the field to come up with the right decision at the time … “[Not having coaching input] is a good thing, and we support that. It gets rid of delays in the game, otherwise you’re waiting for the trainer to run on and get a message. The last thing we want as a game is stoppages like that … Ultimately, it’s fantastic we’re letting the players decide what they are doing.”



Troy Thomson, Brisbane’s manager of football operations, said the rule tweak would provide a lever that could allow momentum to be shifted. “We’ll brief the players and the captain in particular, working through different scenarios,” Thompson said. “If you get scored on, you probably want to get the footy back, particularly if you are chasing points as well. It will depend on the circumstances. If it’s the back end of the game, your tactics and strategy will be very different at the start of the game. It will be quite situational. Dragons captain Damien Cook will play under the new rule in the final-round clash against Parramatta. NRL Photos “It adds another level of strategy for the players.” A point of interest will be whether a team chasing points opts to receive the ball or instead attempts to regather it from a short kick-off. It could also pose a dilemma for teams in front as the clock winds down.



“If you’re protecting a lead with not long to go, sometimes territory is better than possession,” Ponissi explained. “You may as well kick it down [the field], especially with how teams are doing short kick-offs so well. You’d run the threat of losing the ball and giving very good attacking position to the opposition.” The NRL will have a relatively small sample size before deciding to implement the change permanently from next season. The only other confirmed trial in a “dead rubber” is the final-round clash between the Eels and Dragons. “I’m going to want the ball back in my hands if we’ve been scored against to stop the momentum,” said Dragons captain Damien Cook. “A team like Penrith that are very good at their yardage D [defence], they might see a chance to kick off again, lock them back in there and get good field position straight away … “If you’re a team in front and dominating the game, you may want to kick off again. If you’ve got the momentum against you, you probably want the ball back in your hands.”



Related Article NRL 2026 NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night The merits of the change have divided the game. While seven-time premiership-winning coach Wayne Bennett has been a vocal proponent, others believe it is unnecessarily tampering with the fabric of the game. Speaking on Nine’s 100% Footy, Phil Gould and Paul Gallen said they wanted the status quo to remain. “Honestly, this is ridiculous,” Gallen said. “We don’t need all these rule changes. The game’s been so good for such a long time, I don’t get this one.” Gould said that when made in the Super League, the change had only made blowouts worse.



“If you win the toss in a big game, what’s the first thing you say? We’ll kick off. Why? Because it’s easier to get down the other end,” Gould said. “Now you’re going to make it harder for the other team to get down the end.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Albanese and corporate bosses assemble for Business Council dinner
World.content:
Few events in business and politics get the high-calibre turnout that the Business Council of Australia’s annual dinner has come to deliver. And that’s before factoring in the will-he-won’t-he speculation over whether Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn would be among the major corporates to show face for the get-together at the Sofitel Hotel in Sydney’s CBD on Tuesday evening. (To our surprise, Comyn was there.) Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with Business Council of Australia president Geoff Culbert and chief executive Bran Black at the annual BCA dinner. Janie Barrett The guest list had no shortage of talent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was billed as the headline guest, with a gaggle of senior Labor figures in tow. Also from the government, Trade Minister Don Farrell showed up to mingle with execs before the dinner, as did Assistant Science, Technology and Digital Economy Minister Andrew Charlton, and Assistant Productivity Minister Andrew Leigh, who, if our eyes didn’t deceive us, arrived to the ballroom with his backpack slung over his shoulder.



But if reporting from our colleagues on Monday was any indicator, Albanese was no doubt bracing for a tough crowd. The star-studded audience was led by BCA chief executive Bran Black, who was preparing to send the government a warning shot on productivity, according to speech notes reported by this masthead. Bondi Partners founding partner and president Joe Hockey (left) with Business Council of Australia president Geoff Culbert (right). Oscar Colman Our guess is Black will have no shortage of backers for his message. The top executives of Australia’s biggest companies were expected to turn out in force for the annual get-together, including Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady, Coles chief Leah Weckert and representatives from the big four banks. Apart from Comyn, the bankers included NAB chairman Philip Chronican, who was on the list but who we didn’t get eyes on, as well as Westpac chief Anthony Miller and ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos. Also expected were Citi chief executive Mark Woodruff and Macquarie boss ⁠Stuart Green. Public servants were well represented. ASIC chair Sarah Court and ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb were each set to turn out for the function, as was Steven Kennedy, secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, and Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson. Jan Adams, secretary of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, was also expected to go along, as was Department of Climate Change and Energy secretary Mike Kaiser.



With all of these types of functions, there is always a reliable turnout from the hangers-on. So it was little surprise to see former federal treasurer turned Trump whisperer Joe Hockey back on the list this year, along with former defence minister Christopher Pyne. The pair were among the eager and enthusiastic who turned up unfashionably early. (Those relationships aren’t going to cultivate themselves.) A grand final Albo-Kylie tete-a-tete? We should be so lucky It was only last month that Australia discovered Anthony Albanese would “shag” pop icon Kylie Minogue in a game of “shag, marry, date” after the unfortunate revelation emerged on comedian Nikki Osborne’s Bush Deep podcast. The unedifying response has haunted the PM ever since and makes the prospect of Albo potentially crossing paths with Minogue at the AFL grand final at the MCG next month quite delicious. Imagine that tete-a-tete – not awkward at all. Kylie Minogue will perform at the AFL grand final. Getty Images



Minogue, of course, is performing at the grand final’s pre-game show on September 26, and usually the star at the centre of the game day entertainment sticks around for the match. The AFL extends an invitation to the prime minister, various premiers and dignitaries each year as standard practice. Invitations are usually dispatched in early September. But it might be the United Nations, of all things, that stops the meeting of Minogue and Albanese. Loading Albanese is expected to head to New York to attend the high-level General Assembly at the United Nations in the last week of September. While there, he will collect a global citizen gong on the sidelines from the Atlantic Council, which loftily recognises him for “seeking to improve the state of the world”.



CBD put a call into Albanese’s office to work out the odds of an MCG encounter with Kylie. At the time of writing, CBD understands the PM’s travel plans are yet to be determined, so it remains unclear if the grand final will fit into his jet-setting schedule this year. To paraphrase a Minogue hit, we should be so lucky if it did. Elite tennis club starts hunt for another chief Kooyong Lawn Tennis Club is back in the game, finally starting its hunt for a chief executive three months after the sudden departure of its most recent executive leader, Ian Robson. In a note to members on Monday, the club advised it was getting a wriggle on and the search was commencing for “an exceptional leader with the vision, capacity and commitment” to deliver “our long-term strategic objectives”.



Kooyong Lawn Tennis Club is looking for a new chief executive The Age The esteemed tennis establishment has certainly been through the wringer recently. The club’s finances came under scrutiny in 2023 when it was forced to call in independent auditors to investigate millions of dollars in losses from its dining operations. The audit found poor financial management and reporting were to blame for the substantial losses from its dining arm. The club revealed in October last year it was negotiating to buy the nearby Vision Australia premise as part of its Centenary Master Plan to expand its footprint and facilities. That deal fell through in December 2025, and Scotch College is now in talks to buy the Vision Australia head office for about $60 million. Then, at the end of May, club CEO Robson, a former chief executive of Essendon Football Club, departed just 17 months after being appointed.



The club put out its call for new leadership on Seek this week, describing it as a “rare opportunity” to “steward the Club’s next chapter” and “lead the execution of the Club’s strategic vision”. Applications, which close on September 20, and interviews are being managed internally by the club. CBD reached out to the club, hoping to find out if the new boss would be anointed before the Kooyong Classic in January, but didn’t hear back by deadline. Tiley rings the changes in New York Former Tennis Australia boss Craig Tiley is rapidly increasing his profile in his new gig as the head of the United States Tennis Association. The now Florida-based sporting executive rang the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday before the US Open main draw this weekend.



Craig Tiley rings the bell at the New York Stock Exchange. Instagram/@craig_tiley It’s a fair step up from doing the rounds in Melbourne. While his focus might be America these days, Tiley was in the conversation this week about future-proofing Melbourne’s sporting infrastructure. The sporting administrator added his voice to calls for a roofed 20,000 seat multipurpose arena to be built in the Melbourne and Olympic Parks precinct.

World.title: Police cleared of manslaughter over man’s traffic arrest death
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Police cleared of manslaughter over man’s traffic arrest death Tara Cosoleto August 25, 2026 — 7:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Manslaughter charges against two police officers have been thrown out by a magistrate who said the case bore no comparison to the death in the United States of George Floyd. Builder Luke Briggs, 35, died eight days after he was arrested in a convenience store car park at Hoppers Crossing, in Melbourne’s west, in July 2024. Sergeant James Fitzgerald (centre) and Constable Alexander Papanastassis pictured last September. Simon Schluter Constable Alexander Papanastassis, 30, and Sergeant James Fitzgerald, 46, were each charged with negligent manslaughter over the death but fought the charges at a preliminary hearing. Magistrate Patrick Southey determined on Tuesday that there was insufficient evidence for the case to go to trial and dismissed the charges.



“The evidence is so weak that the prospect of a conviction is minimal,” Southey said. “It may be the manner in which Mr Briggs was restrained was the substantial and operative cause of death, but we’ll never know.” Luke Briggs, pictured with sister Catherine, died in July 2024. Briggs became unresponsive during the arrest and the officers performed CPR while waiting for paramedics. The 35-year-old died in hospital on July 23, eight days after his arrest, surrounded by family. Photos at the time showed bruising on his arms as he lay in a hospital bed. In delivering his ruling, Southey referred to the high-profile case of African-American man George Floyd in the US. Floyd was murdered by a white police officer who was arresting him in May 2020.



His dying words of “I can’t breathe” were also said by Briggs, the magistrate noted. “It seems to me the parallels end there,” Southey said. Related Article Victoria Police conduct Family sues police over death of 35-year-old builder in custody “There is no comparison to this case where ... the police were doing the best they could. It was not a perfect job but the best they could do in all the circumstances.” The magistrate noted Briggs was a large, powerful man whose behaviour had been irrational due to methamphetamine use.



“It was an unfortunate, tragic chain of events, but in my view, it does not amount to criminal negligence,” Southey said in the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court. He awarded costs to Papanastassis and Fitzgerald, who have both been suspended from duties since the incident. Members of Briggs’s family were visibly upset as the decision was handed down. Family and friends of Luke Briggs gather to mark the first anniversary of his death. Eddie Jim The family is separately suing the state, accusing the officers of breaching their duty of care and Victoria Police of failing to “properly supervise, control or train their employees, officers and/or agents”.



Police Association secretary Wayne Gatt said the union had stood by the members who had now been rightfully cleared.



“Our members did their job. A difficult job, a challenging job, a dynamic job, and one that places them squarely between criminal behaviour and community safety,” he said.



“That night, they did what any of their colleagues would have done. They pulled over a suspicious vehicle and attempted to speak to the driver. When the situation escalated into a physical confrontation, they tried to manage it peacefully, but they were not afforded that opportunity.” AAP

World.title: Rabbitoh closes in on three-year deal; concussed Radley set to miss rest of regular season
World.content:
Tallis Duncan says he is ready to shift back to his preferred back-row position to accommodate Latrell Mitchell as he prepares to sign off on a contract extension that is set to keep him at the club until the end 2030. Duncan has been impressive in the centres in the three months Mitchell has been sidelined with injury. Tallis Duncan is a star on the rise at Souths. Getty Images Mitchell, who has had nerve issues in his lower back and related problems in his leg and calf, was named in the No.19 jersey for Saturday’s clash against the Gold Coast. Duncan, 24, has been one of the Bunnies’ best this season, and his form is expected to be rewarded with a new three-year deal.



The 24-year-old was ready to attract plenty of interest had he remained a free agent until November 1, but made it clear he was only interested in remaining in the red and green – and there was one rival club he would never entertain. “I want to be here, this is where I want to be – I see myself as a South Sydney player for a long time,” Duncan said. Loading “I was a Roosters junior, but [a return to the Roosters] won’t be happening. There’s some history there. I won’t say too much about it, but that won’t happen.” Duncan said Mitchell’s impending return to the line-up would give the Bunnies a timely boost leading into a likely finals campaign. “It’s massive for us as a club,” Duncan said. “You know what he brings: his presence, he brings confidence [to the rest of us]. He’s the ace up our sleeve.”



Meanwhile, Roosters skipper James Tedesco (ankle) has been named to return from an ankle injury for Saturday’s match of the round against the Dolphins, with Nat Butcher to start at lock for Victor Radley. Radley suffered his eighth concussion in five years during the shock loss to the Wests Tigers and will miss the Dolphins blockbuster due to the NRL’s mandatory 11-day stand-down, but was in good spirits at training on Tuesday. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 ‘I’ll cry my eyes out’: Jai Arrow will take the field for South Sydney again. Expect tears Daly Cherry-Evans said Radley’s latest head knock may even prove a blessing for the no-nonsense forward. “He was fine today, which is a really good sign,” Cherry-Evans said. “I know he’s in very good hands at this club. The Roosters take a lot of pride in how they handle serious situations like head injuries. There are no short-cuts or sweeping anything under the carpet – it’s always about the best interests of the player.



“It’s a case-by-case scenario, but I’ve heard ‘Robbo’ [coach Trent Robinson] talk about it publicly before, and he’s really clear on how it should be handled. “Rads is a leader of our side, he’s one of the elite locks in the game. We know how classy his ball playing is, but his defence this year has been great for us. If it’s not as bad as like he was telling me this morning, that’s a great freshen-up for Rads going into the finals.” Radley sidelined with concussion Christian Nicolussi Victor Radley looks set to be sidelined until the finals after suffering a concussion during the Roosters’ stunning 25-24 loss to Wests Tigers on Sunday.



The Roosters confirmed on Monday Radley had displayed category one symptoms after a heavy collision, which means he will need to stand down for the next 11 days. Loading Radley went low on Tigers forward Alex Seyfarth and wobbled back into the defensive line before referee Ashley Klein realised the seriousness of the situation and sent him for a head injury assessment. The tackle happened in the 79th minute, just before Jock Madden kicked the match-winning field goal, meaning Radley’s condition was missed by many observers at full-time. Fans initially feared Radley would miss Saturday’s clash with the Dolphins due to a high tackle on Patrick Herbert. He was charged by the match review committee on Monday but only fined $3000.



But the concussion will mean he misses the Dolphins clash and most likely the round-27 showdown with South Sydney on Friday week. Victor Radley comes from the field after being concussed against the Broncos in 2025. Getty Images Given his long history of head knocks – Sunday was his eighth concussion or failed HIA in five years – Radley will now be required to gain a clearance from an independent doctor to play again. The Roosters have adopted an ultra-conservative approach with players returning from concussions, including Lindsay Collins, who was given six weeks to recover earlier this season – a break which also cost him a chance to play for Queensland in the Origin decider. Related Article NRL 2026 NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night



Skipper and fullback James Tedesco is hoping to return from an ankle injury for the Allianz Stadium hit-out, which the Dolphins need to win to remain in the top four. Radley last year said he had no plans to retire early, revealing he met with several specialists and even started playing memory games twice a day to “work” his brain. “I’ve got no worries whatsoever with my head,” Radley said at the time. The 28-year-old Bronte local is eager to help the Roosters win the premiership, then turn his attention to helping England win the World Cup. Siua Wong was also charged with a careless high tackle on Jock Madden, but can also escape with a fine, while Reece Robson and Daly Cherry-Evans were not cited by the match review committee, despite being placed on report for a high tackle and trip.



Ten Dogs struck down by COVID Dan Walsh Ten Bulldogs NRL squad members – headlined by star back-rower Jacob Preston – were kept away from the club training on Monday as a COVID-19 outbreak threatens to derail the biggest week of Canterbury’s season. Just five days out from Friday’s must-win clash against powerhouse Penrith, the Bulldogs trained without more than a quarter of their NRL squad (which includes top 30 and development players) after a spate of positive COVID-19 tests among their players. Preston was the most notable absentee, while fellow forwards Josh Curran and Kurt Mann were also missing – though Mann was carrying a groin injury that was expected to rule him out of selection against the Panthers. Not all the players taken ill are first-graders.



Assistant coach Adam O’Brien was also told to stay at home after flu ripped through the club for a second straight week. Jacob Preston in action against the Dragons on Saturday night. NRL Photos Preston’s positive COVID-19 test came after the barnstorming second-rower spent time in hospital on a drip last week due to an elbow infection, in the days leading into the 44-14 win over St George Illawarra that kept Canterbury’s season alive. Coach Cameron Ciraldo revealed after downing the Dragons match that five players had missed training throughout the week due to COVID-19 as well. It is unclear at this stage how the outbreak will impact Ciraldo’s team list announcement for the Panthers clash, which must be announced at 4pm on Tuesday, but the club is taking no chances and keeping any player showing symptoms away from their Belmore base.



The ninth-placed Bulldogs will have their main field session on Wednesday. Winger Enari Tuala, who was a late scratching last week with a knee injury, is expected to return against the Panthers, while Jacob Kiraz continues to push through a calf injury. Loading With two rounds left in the regular season, a loss to Penrith would almost certainly end Canterbury’s hopes of sneaking into the top eight given the Cowboys (eighth) and South Sydney (seventh) already sit two points ahead of them on the ladder. Last year’s corresponding clash between the sides saw Panthers coach Ivan Cleary rest his entire first choice teams. Related Article Opinion

But with Penrith still fighting to secure a home final, Cleary will name his best line-up on Friday night before weighing up whether to do the same a week later against the Tigers in the last game of the regular season. Jack Cole is expected to replace suspended five-eighth Jack Cogger against the Bulldogs given Blaize Talagi’s defensive frailties were exposed by Canterbury’s right edge earlier this year.

World.title: Youths on proposed social media ban: Cautious approval, but questions around enforcement
World.content:
Young people question proposed social media ban Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

"How are you going to enforce this?" That's the response from young people who grew up with social media to the proposed ban for under-16s.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media is exposing young people to harmful content, addictive technology and pressure they aren't equipped to deal with, and the government would push ahead with the Online Safety Bill.

"We would never knowingly let our children wander into places in the real world we know to be unsafe. We put boundaries around cars, around alcohol, around gambling, because we know children aren't yet equipped for them."

So, it has been proposed that social media platforms will risk financial penalties if they don't take steps to verify the age of users.

But some Auckland 17- and 18-year-olds say they're not convinced a complete ban will work.

For some teens who jumped on to social media around 12 years old, some of what the government mentioned during their announcement resembled their experiences.

Checkpoint spoke with some Year 13 students from Auckland's Albany Senior High School.

Jeremy Ouwejan said he often saw content that came from online communities such as the manosphere.

"Andrew Tate speaking to young impressionable men about very damaging ideologies like misogyny, transphobia and homophobia, or, armchair psychology that says how to manipulate your friends and how to do certain things.

Andrew Tate. AFP / DANIEL MIHAILESCU

"Or people will say, 'I used to be a dietitian, here's what you should and shouldn't eat.' [Instagram] Reels on working out and harmful gym content saying, 'If you're not benching 100kg are you even a real person?'"

Ouwejan said he also had seen posts that were violent.

"I'll hop onto Reels and I'll be flashed with a [dead] body. It'll completely ruin the experience of just wanting to talk to a friend."

Last year, research from Te Mana Whakaatu / The Classification Office, found young people don't generally go looking for objectionable content. But it could be hard to avoid when it came up on social media, in group chats or was shown around in person.

Some examples of this included pornography and real-world violence.

Another student, Natalie Osmond, told Checkpoint coming across extreme, violent and misogynistic content every day took a toll.

"When you're giving people ranked numerical scores, especially women… it's objectification to the highest level. You can't just put a number value on someone, it's bad it comes with the podcasts.

"A lot of my feed is about Ariana Grande for example, and other female artists. The [comments] will be all about body image and they're just saying horrible things."

Ariana Grande. CHRIS DELMAS

But, she said, social media also came with its positives.

"Social media is also a good way to get informed from people. There's a fine line between getting informed and seeing all of the bad stuff.

"I do think it's a crazy time to be alive and we can see what's going on in any corner of the world."

Osmond agreed restricting some parts of social media and having consequences for creating or promoting harmful content was a good thing.

"I wish it was socially acceptable to have a Nokia brick - I know I could actually do that, but I really couldn't.

"Also, even as a child I remember being 12 years old and it would socially stunt you even if you weren't allowed social media... you're pressured to have it from a very young age."

But Osmond and the other students Checkpoint spoke to weren't convinced a ban would work, with reports from Australia of teens using loopholes to get around it.

Ouwejan said change was needed, but had to be thought through.

"I think currently there is a lot of very young people on some very damaging platforms, and it is changing them for the worse for the rest of their lives.

"However, as we have seen from Australia and what we can interpolate from other studies and other bans, banning is not the way to go - we need a controlled method, but balancing that with free speech."

Another student, Isabella Green, said she was concerned around how the government would enforce a ban.

"How are you going to track and enforce this? That doesn't feel like it's something that would respect the privacy of people."

ACT and New Zealand First will not support the bill, meaning National will need Labour's support if it's to progress.

Not enough evidence - commissioner

Doubts over whether social media ban is enforceable Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle told Checkpoint more evidence into the effectiveness of a complete ban was needed before implementing one in Aotearoa.

"We know that [kids have told] us that they want the internet to be made safer or online harm to be reduced for them. Whether the solution is just in a complete ban, that remains to be seen, and we need to look at the evidence around that."

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle. Stephen Barker / Barker Photography via Child Matters

Searle said that a more comprehensive plan to tackle the issues around social media was needed, rather than just an outright ban.

"I think that we need good education for young people and their families to be able to make good decisions that keep them safe. But we also need to be able to hold tech companies to account and have robust obligations on them.

"Then we need to look at the regulation - do we have an independent regulator?"

She said there was also a concern over young people who may be marginalised or isolated as the result of a ban.

"We need to be very careful when we move forward, and we need to look at the evidence. We need to know, what will this ban look like in practice? How will it actually impact the way that young people are engaging with social media?"

Searle said there wasn't currently enough information to know if a ban would be successful.

"Even if you look at other countries, what they've implemented, it wasn't long ago, so we don't have that evidence to know."

She said more onus needed to be put on social media companies to manage what content they were showing to young people.

"It's about how they design the algorithms, how they engage with young people, how they put checks in places on what age and what is age appropriate."

However, she acknowledged that enforcing regulations on large tech companies would be difficult.

"I think we need to try and we need to put as much in place as possible. And then hopefully we can work with other governments around the world to actually have some influence as well."

World.title: Man found guilty of threatening to kill people at two Auckland schools
World.content:
A man has been found guilty of threatening to kill people at two Auckland schools and saying he would destroy police stations and buildings at Parliament.

A jury in the Manukau District Court today found Tiedan Huo guilty of 12 charges relating to threats against Waiuku and Rutherford colleges and other public buildings.

Huo was also convicted for unlawful possession of a firearm, unlawful possession of explosives and possession of objectionable material.

Huo denied all charges and mid-way through the trial elected to act for himself in place of the lawyers who had been acting for him.

The charges stemmed from a manifesto, in which he spoke of using 3D-printed firearms in an attack.

The jury took just under three hours to find him guilty on all charges.

In his opening address to the jury, Crown prosecutor Gareth Kayes said that on 12 March last year, staff at Waiuku College woke to a chilling email that had been sent at 1.42am.

"It was titled 'Important: Don't come to school tomorrow'. And it started with the words 'This is my manifesto'."

The email spoke of being bullied and humiliated by teachers at the school, being unfairly treated by police and being made to feel like a second-class citizen for being Chinese.

"I am going to do something about this now. I have began [sic] preparing for doing something about this since February this year and have finished now."

The email went on to set out in some detail the preparations the sender said they had made to carry out attacks on Waiuku and Rutherford colleges, as well as damaging the Pukekohe and Te Atatu police stations and buildings at Parliament.

That included making firearms using a 3D printer and creating bullets and explosives to be used in an attack.

The sender said they wanted to kill more people than the Christchurch mosque terrorist, who murdered 51 innocent people on 15 March 2019.

"Do not assume that my guns will not work or are fake because they are 3D printed, that will be very bad."

The email was purportedly sent by a female former Waiuku College student, but after she allowed police to examine her electronic devices, officers established this was not the case, and their inquiries led them to Huo.

World.title: Warriors call on debutant Luke Laulilii for Knights clash
World.content:
The ladder-leading Warriors have called up a debutant to replace their injured winger as they chase a second NRL minor premiership.

The Warriors have made three changes for Sunday's round 26 game against the Newcastle Knights including the addition of right winger Luke Laulilii who comes in for Dallin Watene-Zelezniak.

Watene-Zelezniak crossed for his 20th try of the season in Saturday's 45-26 win over South Sydney but it was later revealed he had played on for a spell after breaking his collarbone during a dive near the corner flag.

Laulilii will become the Warriors' 300th NRL player after signing from the Wests Tigers in June.

The 20-year-old scored 10 tries in 17 NRL appearances for his former club.

In six New South Wales Cup outings since joining the Warriors. he has averaged 180 metres a game, scored two tries and made 22 tackle breaks.

Halfback Te Maire Martin comes back from injury for the sold-out game at Go Media Stadium after missing the last three matches with a hamstring injury.

Te Maire Martin is one of three changes for the Warriors against the Knights. David Neilson/Photosport

He's reunited in the halves with his regular partner Chanel Harris-Tavita who filled in at halfback for 60 minutes against the Broncos and then started at No. 7 for the first time since 2021 in the Rabbitoh's game.

As well as Martin, regular right edge centre Ali Leiataua is back after missing the South Sydney encounter through illness.

The Warriors go into the contest leading the competition, one of three teams on 38 points but narrowly ahead of second-placed Penrith on points for and against.

At the business end of the season, the Warriors have qualified for the NRL playoffs 10 times in their 31-season history but have only claimed one minor premiership, in 2002, when they pipped the Knights on points differential.

World.title: National MPs 'misappropriate' time for questions in the House
World.content:
National is being accused of making a mockery of Parliament's processes by deliberately not giving itself enough time to answer questions from Opposition MPs in the House.

Leader of the House Louise Upston says National has tried to fix the system to ensure that does not happen, but not all parties agreed on proposed changes.

In the House on Tuesday, MPs took part in the Estimates debate, which scrutinises Budget spending decisions.

The debate runs for 11 hours over a number of sitting days.

Each party is given a certain amount of time to speak, spread across the course of the debate, and the party whips allocate that time between their members.

Nearing the end of the debate on Tuesday afternoon, Upston - in her capacity as Social Development Minister - refused to continue answering questions because her time allocation was up.
